problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}].$

examples.problem:
Given the matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/8921e351c90855b6bf113a057eaa7e3ab97fbba8f22254463d894e7c4f89a4ed.png) 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D=P^{-1}AP.$
examples.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm. 

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$$
\lambda_1=3, \quad\quad\lambda_2=-2.
$$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the corresponding system of linear equations, we construct the augmented matrix $M$ and reduce it to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-\frac{5}{8}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). So, $x_1$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_2=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/ff2073ee3866cfd3b40084ed4e676cc57554d9cd02b9d6e26cb7808f127fc56c.png)
Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/55c840d71fa907a9b372801123fdc7f19be810f2f489a2b167b0860c84d1c2cc.png)

- For $\lambda_2=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The above matrix corresponds to a homogeneous system of linear equations. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=\dfrac{8}{5}x_2.$ Therefore, the general solution is

Setting  $x_2=5,$ we get the eigenvector  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/ebb90bd7e57a148040b69a9fd6fd7d4f1b253e63734617e4e57b5177d7f9cda9.png)

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

feedback.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -12 \\ 6 & -10\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & a \\ 2 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\frac{a}{b}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ 

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ Computing $A-2I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -12 \\ 6 & -10\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -12 \\ 6 & -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -12 \\ 6 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & -12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{2}{1}=2.$
